system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

Each turn shows the current state of the investigation, including what you already tried. Do not repeat a call listed there.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
final.target_customer: German EV owners planning home charging within 12 months who value automotive-grade performance and are willing to pay a premium for reliability.
final.value_proposition: A premium home EV heater marketed as automotive-grade, offering superior performance and reliability, sold through specialty retailers at a 20% price premium over generic alternatives.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 300 German EV owners, to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the premium and specialized concepts.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence that consumers will adopt a premium proposition or that compatibility is the primary purchase driver. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion.

X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer purchase decisions, brand trust, or compatibility preferences for a home EV charging use case. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
final.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
final.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence that consumers value brand trust or compatibility enough to pay a premium. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the premium product ≥ 45% and for the specialized product ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows the opposite (e.g., specialized ≥ 45%, premium ≤ 35%), we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
final.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
final.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence that consumers value brand trust or compatibility enough to pay a premium. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the premium product ≥ 45% and for the specialized product ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows the opposite (e.g., specialized ≥ 45%, premium ≤ 35%), we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Generic Drill Bits
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 200 hobbyists and small workshop owners recruited via metalworking forums and social media, balanced across Germany and the US.
X1.measure: 1) Choice: which drill bit they would purchase (Gühring premium or generic alternative). 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for the chosen brand. 3) Quality ranking (1‑10) for each brand.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of respondents will choose Gühring premium and indicate intent to purchase, with a WTP premium of at least 20% over generic.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% will choose Gühring premium and indicate intent to purchase, with a WTP premium of at least 15% over generic, achieved via existing B2B channels.

X1.decision_rule: If the observed choice rate for Gühring premium ≥ 40% and the average WTP premium ≥ 20% (or 15% via B2B channel), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If either condition fails, recommend no expansion.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference test (X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a Gühring premium drill bit before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Hobbyists and small workshops who perform metalworking projects and require precision tools.
final.value_proposition: A Gühring premium drill bit that delivers superior accuracy, durability, and brand reputation, sold directly through the existing online shop at a modest premium over generic alternatives.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 consumer preference test (X1) with 200 hobbyists and small workshop owners to measure choice, willingness to pay, and quality ranking for Gühring premium versus generic.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence that hobbyists are aware of Gühring’s brand or that they purchase tools through its B2B channels. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows at least 40% choice for Gühring premium and a willingness‑to‑pay premium of at least 20% over generic, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists.
If the test shows Gühring premium is not preferred or the premium is below 15%, abandon the consumer expansion and focus on B2B growth.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Generic Drill Bits
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 200 hobbyists and small workshop owners recruited via metalworking forums and social media, balanced across Germany and the US.
arguments.measure: 1) Choice: which drill bit they would purchase (Gühring premium or generic alternative). 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for the chosen brand. 3) Quality ranking (1‑10) for each brand.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of respondents will choose Gühring premium and indicate intent to purchase, with a WTP premium of at least 20% over generic.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% will choose Gühring premium and indicate intent to purchase, with a WTP premium of at least 15% over generic, achieved via existing B2B channels.

arguments.decision_rule: If the observed choice rate for Gühring premium ≥ 40% and the average WTP premium ≥ 20% (or 15% via B2B channel), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If either condition fails, recommend no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Gühring KG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial metal machining tools, and identify what evidence would support that investment.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring can capture value through premium pricing, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand positioning that differentiates its tools from generic alternatives.
assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops have access to Gühring’s online shop or other direct‑to‑consumer channels.
They evaluate tools based on precision, durability, and application‑specific features.
They are willing to pay more for tools that meet their demanding criteria.
predictions: In a test offering Gühring tools at a 20‑30% premium price to hobbyists, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a generic competitor offering equivalent tools.
Customer surveys will indicate that accuracy and reliability are key purchase drivers for this segment.

X1.measure: 1) Maximum price participants would pay for a Gühring drill bit (WTP). 2) Choice between a premium-priced version (20‑30% above standard price) emphasizing precision and professional‑grade performance, and a status‑branded version (15‑20% above standard price) emphasizing prestige and community affiliation. prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants will choose the premium version because they value precision and are willing to pay more for it.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants will choose the status version because they value brand prestige and community affiliation, even if the price is higher.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion choosing the premium version ≥ 55% and the proportion choosing the status version ≤ 45%, then T1 is supported. If the reverse, T2 is supported. If neither reaches 55% for its respective version, the test is inconclusive.

final.target_customer: Hobbyists and small workshops (DIY metalworking, home CNC mills) who purchase tools for personal projects.
final.value_proposition: A Gühring consumer line that emphasizes precision, reliability, and professional‑grade performance, sold at a premium price through direct‑to‑consumer channels.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 conjoint survey with 200 participants to measure choice between precision‑focused and status‑branded versions.

arguments.name: Premium vs Status Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 200 hobbyists and small workshop owners (recruited via metalworking forums, social media, and DIY communities) who have purchased metalworking tools in the past 12 months.
arguments.measure: 1) Maximum price participants would pay for a Gühring drill bit (WTP). 2) Choice between a premium-priced version (20‑30% above standard price) emphasizing precision and professional‑grade performance, and a status‑branded version (15‑20% above standard price) emphasizing prestige and community affiliation. prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants will choose the premium version because they value precision and are willing to pay more for it.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants will choose the status version because they value brand prestige and community affiliation, even if the price is higher.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion choosing the premium version ≥ 55% and the proportion choosing the status version ≤ 45%, then T1 is supported. If the reverse, T2 is supported. If neither reaches 55% for its respective version, the test is inconclusive.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Krones homebrew machine (specifying premium features, convenience, or scalability) and are asked: (1) Maximum price they would pay; (2) Likelihood to purchase; (3) Likelihood to recommend to friends. Survey also captures demographic and homebrew experience.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. homebrewers recruited via brewing forums and social media, balanced for experience level and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Average maximum price willing to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1-10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average maximum price willing to pay will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable generic homebrew kit (e.g., $338 vs $299). Purchase intent will be above 6/10.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average maximum price willing to pay will be at least 30% above the price of a comparable generic homebrew kit. Purchase intent will be above 6/10.

frame.objective: Determine whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial B2B focus, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view charging as a friction point and Lapp offers a solution that eliminates or reduces that friction, they will switch from generic accessories to Lapp, driven by perceived convenience and reliability.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp would sell premium-priced charging kits directly to consumers through its own e-commerce or retail channels, earning higher margins than bulk B2B sales.

Lapp can design a product that significantly reduces installation time or provides a unique convenience feature.
Lapp’s existing distribution network can reach private buyers without major changes.
predictions: A test offering a convenience-focused charging kit to a sample of private EV owners will achieve a purchase rate of at least 15% within 12 weeks.

X1.name: Convenience vs Incentive Messaging Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized messaging.
X1.sample: 500 private EV owners recruited via panel, balanced by age, gender, and region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: stated primary reason for choosing Lapp (convenience vs incentive).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent when presented with a convenience-focused description (e.g., "easy installation, fast charging, smart home integration").
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent when presented with an incentive-focused description (e.g., "government subsidy of 20% off").

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for convenience messaging >= 30% AND purchase intent for incentive messaging >= 30%, both theories are considered plausible. If only one meets the threshold, the corresponding theory is supported. If neither meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Convenience vs Incentive Messaging Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under convenience and incentive messaging. If both meet the 30% threshold, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience; otherwise, reconsider expansion or focus on existing B2B markets.
final.target_customer: Private electric car owners who install charging accessories at home.
final.value_proposition: A convenience-focused charging kit that eliminates installation friction (e.g., plug-and-play, smart home integration) and is sold directly to consumers at a premium price, leveraging Lapp’s existing global sales network.
final.next_action: Execute the 12‑week online conjoint survey with 500 EV owners, allocate €15,000 for the test, and analyze purchase intent and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: The test is uncertain because it does not directly measure willingness to pay for convenience; it only tests perceived intent. Additionally, the existence and impact of government incentives vary across markets.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for convenience messaging below 30% or if incentive messaging achieves higher intent, the favoured theory would shift and the recommendation would change to prioritize incentive-driven expansion.

Both descriptions include price point (€200). Participants indicate whether they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. The
X1.sample: 500 German adults aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year, recruited via an online panel.

final.target_customer: German home cooks aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey (X1) to test whether consumers will pay a premium for a professional-grade vacuum sealer versus a health-focused one. The test will decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks, or to remain focused on B2B packaging equipment.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, small‑batch medical supplies) with a new product or service.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical, pharmaceutical, and industrial producers.

T1.claim: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a professional-grade tool that improves food freshness and reduces waste, leading to multiple purchases per household.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to preserve food quality and save money; MULTIVAC benefits by capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in sous vide cooking and bulk food processing creates a demand for reliable, airtight sealing; current chamber sealers are already used by professional chefs and home enthusiasts, signaling quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC can price the consumer model at a premium (e.g., €200-€300) and sell accessories (bags, seals) and service contracts, generating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Home users have sufficient disposable income to justify the price.
Marketing can effectively communicate professional-grade performance.
Distribution channels (online, specialty retailers) can reach target consumers.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer.
Purchase intent will be higher when described as a professional-grade tool.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months.

T2.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC can market the consumer model as a health‑preserving tool, price it at a premium (e.g., €200‑€300), and sell accessories and subscription services for reusable bags, capturing recurring revenue.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for products that reduce waste.
Marketing can effectively communicate nutrient retention benefits.
Distribution can reach health‑focused consumers (specialty retailers, online health platforms).
predictions: Surveyed health‑conscious consumers will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer marketed on nutrient retention.
Purchase intent will be higher when highlighted as a waste‑reducing solution.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months when positioned as health‑focused.

final.target_customer: German home cooks aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year and are interested in sous vide cooking or bulk food processing.
final.value_proposition: A consumer vacuum sealer marketed as a professional-grade tool for sous vide and bulk food processing, priced at €200, with accessories and service contracts, capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases.
final.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €15,000 survey with 500 participants, presenting two product descriptions and measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a targeted test (e.g., the proposed consumer preference test) to validate demand and willingness to pay for a premium, integrated smart storage system before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a specific consumer use case.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential partner/distribution relationships.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home storage, small‑business inventory management).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., food‑processing, e‑commerce fulfillment) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion – maintain current product and market focus, monitor consumer trends without investment.
4) License Kardex’s technology to consumer brands or white‑label solutions for consumer markets.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage primarily if the solution is marketed as a premium, integrated smart system that solves a specific pain point (e.g., space optimization or inventory management) and is delivered through a dedicated consumer brand and direct-to-consumer channels.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking efficient storage solutions and Kardex through premium pricing and brand equity in a new consumer segment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers increasingly seek integrated smart home solutions that automate and optimize daily tasks; a differentiated proposition that addresses a clear consumer need and is positioned as a premium, easy-to-use product will attract those who
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex captures value through higher margins from direct-to-consumer sales, subscription services for software/data, and optional add‑ons, leveraging existing manufacturing capabilities to produce a consumer‑specific product.
assumptions: There is sufficient consumer awareness and willingness to pay for automated home storage solutions.
Kardex can adapt its existing manufacturing and service infrastructure to serve the consumer market.
Distribution partners will be willing to take on a consumer brand and dedicated sales channels.
predictions: A consumer proposition marketed as a premium smart storage system will achieve at least 10% higher willingness-to-pay than comparable non-smart storage products.
Purchase intent will be higher among households with a higher proportion of tech‑savvy occupants (e.g., millennials) or those seeking space optimization.
Repeat purchase rate for subscription services (e.g., data management or software updates) will be at least 30% within 12 months of initial purchase.

T2.who_benefits: Kardex through access to established consumer markets and brand trust, and the consumer brand through a new, low-cost entry into automated storage.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers already shop at these brands and trust their product quality; bundling a storage solution with a familiar brand reduces perceived risk and simplifies purchase decisions, especially for
T2.how_value_is_captured: Kardex captures value through volume sales at lower margins but higher unit volume, and through optional add-ons or service contracts; the consumer brand captures value through new product category and potential cross-selling.
assumptions: The consumer brand is willing to partner with Kardex to co-brand a storage solution.
Kardex can meet the brand’s quality and design standards for a consumer product.
Consumers will purchase the bundled product at a price point that covers Kardex’s cost and generates a modest margin for the brand.
predictions: A bundled consumer proposition will achieve at least 20% higher purchase intent than a standalone Kardex product offered through the same channel.
The bundled product will be purchased by at least 15% of households that have previously purchased products from the partnering brand.
Repeat purchase rate for add-ons or service contracts will be at least 25% within 12 months of initial purchase.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view two versions of a Nabtesco automatic door product description: (1) Safety/Rehabilitation version emphasizing enhanced safety and accessibility for users with limited mobility; (2) Convenience version emphasizing time savings and ease of use for homeowners. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 200 homeowners (100 per version) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent score (1‑10) for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the safety/rehabilitation version than for the convenience version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the convenience version than for the safety/rehabilitation version.

frame.objective: Determine whether Nabtesco Corporation should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B product portfolio, and identify evidence that would justify such an investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current product range includes precision reduction gears, automatic doors, transport equipment, welfare components, and packaging machines.
Customer base primarily consists of manufacturers, building owners, transport operators, and equipment manufacturers.
Uncertainty about current individual buyer reach and existing consumer products.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home automation, personal mobility, or wellness).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., consumer robotics, smart home devices, or consumer packaging).
3) Maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue any consumer expansion.
4) License Nabtesco’s technology to consumer brands rather than selling under its own brand.
5) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute consumer‑focused products.

assumptions: Consumers in target markets are willing to pay a premium for perceived innovation.
Marketing can effectively communicate the technology story to individual buyers.
Nabtesco can scale production to meet higher-margin premium segments without compromising quality.
predictions: In a test offering two identical automatic door models, the premium model will achieve a higher average price point and higher purchase intent among surveyed consumers.
Surveyed consumers will rank Nabtesco higher on a technology brand perception scale compared to competitors offering identical doors.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a voice-controlled automatic door kit for residential use. They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) standard description emphasizing affordability, ease of installation, and smart home compatibility; (B) description also mentioning a government subsidy or tax credit for energy-efficient home automation. After reading the description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and state the maximum price they would pay. The test is run with 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel, each receiving a €10 incentive.
X1.sample: 300 adult homeowners in Germany and France who have installed smart home devices in their homes.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).

They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) standard description emphasizing affordability, ease of installation, and smart home compatibility; (B) description also mentioning a government subsidy or tax credit for energy-efficient home automation. The test is run with 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel, each receiving a €10 incentive.

position.recommendation: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. frame.objective: Determine whether Biesse S.p.A. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify such an investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual details may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current revenue is predominantly from abroad; any new consumer proposition must consider existing B2B relationships and market presence.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to individual buyers for the proposed use case.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY wood processing, home‑scale glass cutting) with a new product or service.

2) Expand existing B2B offerings into new segments or geographies without creating a distinct consumer proposition (e.g., deeper penetration of furniture manufacturers, entry into new construction markets).
3) No expansion: maintain current product and market focus, focusing resources on existing B2B customers and existing product lines.
4) License Biesse technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Biesse's own consumer brand.
5) Partner with retailers or e‑commerce platforms to co‑brand consumer‑friendly products for existing B2B customers' end‑users.

X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for a Consumer-Grade Biesse CNC Router
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY woodworkers (defined as those who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months) and homeowners (defined as those who have undertaken home improvement projects requiring precision cutting). Each participant is shown a product description of a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router with specifications matching a desktop model (e.g., 12"x24" work
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 DIY woodworkers and 100 homeowners. Recruitment via a panel provider to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros, measured as the maximum price participants would pay for the router. Secondary measures: purchase intent (binary) and perceived importance of precision and professional-grade features.

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY woodworkers will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for DIY woodworkers exceeds €2,000 and the average WTP for homeowners exceeds €2,000, both theories are considered supported. If only one group exceeds €2,000, the theory for that group is supported, and the other is rejected. If neither group exceeds €2,000, both theories are rejected.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. The survey will provide real demand evidence and help decide whether to invest in a differentiated consumer proposition or pursue other options.
final.target_customer: DIY woodworkers who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months and are willing to purchase directly from Biesse.
final.value_proposition: A consumer-grade Biesse CNC router that delivers professional-grade precision and digital control, sold directly to DIY woodworkers at a premium price, capturing margin on hardware and software while offering accessories and service
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 willingness‑to‑pay survey with 200 participants (100 DIY woodworkers, 100 homeowners). Analyze results against the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition or explore
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on DIY woodworker demand and willingness to pay a premium for a consumer‑grade router. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay below €2,000 for DIY woodworkers, T1 would be rejected and the recommendation would shift to other expansion options or no expansion.
If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay above €2,000 for homeowners, T2 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to targeting homeowners instead of DIY woodworkers.

frame.objective: Determine whether Biesse S.p.A. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify such an investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual details may not be available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY wood processing, home‑scale glass cutting) with a new product or service.

2) Expand existing B2B offerings into new segments or geographies without creating a distinct consumer proposition (e.g., deeper penetration of furniture manufacturers, entry into new construction markets).
3) No expansion: maintain current product and market focus, focusing resources on existing B2B customers and existing product lines.
4) License Biesse technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Biesse's own consumer brand.
5) Partner with retailers or e‑commerce platforms to co‑brand consumer‑friendly products for existing B2B customers' end‑users.

X1.name: Digital Precision Preference Test
X1.method: Online choice experiment with between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to view a product description of a Biesse‑branded CNC router, either emphasizing professional‑grade accuracy and intuitive control (T1), or emphasizing home‑use versatility and brand trust (T2). Both versions include the same technical specifications (e.g., precision tolerance, spindle speed) and a price point 20% above Biesse’s
X1.sample: 300 participants: 200 DIY woodworkers (recruited via woodworking forums and social media) and 100 professional woodworkers (recruited via woodworking schools and industry associations). Each participant receives a unique link to the survey.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: “Would you buy this router?” (Yes/No). Secondary measures: willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale and time spent viewing the product description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY woodworkers will show purchase intent ≥ 15% and professional woodworkers will show purchase intent ≤ 5%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional woodworkers will show purchase intent ≥ 15% and DIY woodworkers will show purchase intent ≤ 5%.

X1.decision_rule: If DIY purchase intent ≥ 15% and professional purchase intent ≤ 5% → adopt T1. If professional purchase intent ≥ 15% and DIY purchase intent ≤ 5% → adopt T2. If neither condition met → inconclusive.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer purchase behavior, professional woodworker demand, or brand perception. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Digital Precision Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent among DIY woodworkers exposed to a professional‑grade accuracy description versus a home‑use versatility description. The test will determine whether the market is driven by professional‑grade demand (T1) or by brand trust and home‑use need (T2). Until results are available, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor
final.target_customer: DIY woodworkers (hobbyists, small‑batch craftspeople) who need precise cutting for personal projects and small‑batch production.
final.value_proposition: A Biesse‑branded CNC router that delivers professional‑grade accuracy and intuitive control, sold through retail or online channels at a premium price, capturing recurring revenue from service and maintenance.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week, €15,000 choice experiment (X1) with 300 participants (200 DIY woodworkers, 100 professional woodworkers). Measure purchase intent, willingness to pay, and time spent viewing product descriptions.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is limited public evidence on DIY woodworker demand for a Biesse‑branded router and no direct sales data. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows DIY purchase intent ≥15% and professional intent ≤5% (supporting T1), proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on professional‑grade accuracy.
If the test shows professional intent ≥15% and DIY intent ≤5% (supporting T2), explore a consumer proposition emphasizing home‑use versatility and brand trust.
If neither condition is met, the evidence would be inconclusive and the recommendation would remain to maintain the current B2B focus.

arguments.name: Digital Precision Preference Test
arguments.method: Online choice experiment with between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to view a product description of a Biesse‑branded CNC router, either emphasizing professional‑grade accuracy and intuitive control (T1), or emphasizing home‑use versatility and brand trust (T2). Both versions include the same technical specifications (e.g., precision tolerance, spindle speed) and a price point 20% above Biesse’s
arguments.sample: 300 participants: 200 DIY woodworkers (recruited via woodworking forums and social media) and 100 professional woodworkers (recruited via woodworking schools and industry associations). Each participant receives a unique link to the survey.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: “Would you buy this router?” (Yes/No). Secondary measures: willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale and time spent viewing the product description.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Brembo investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B and aftermarket offerings, and identify what evidence would support that investment.

4) License Brembo’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under its own brand.

X1.sample: 500 motorcycle enthusiasts (recruited via motorcycle forums and social media) and 500 eco-conscious consumers (recruited via environmental advocacy groups and sustainability-focused websites). Stratify by region (Italy, Germany, UK, US) to reflect market diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would purchase within 12 weeks") and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).

arguments.sample: 500 motorcycle enthusiasts (recruited via motorcycle forums and social media) and 500 eco-conscious consumers (recruited via environmental advocacy groups and sustainability-focused websites). Stratify by region (Italy, Germany, UK, US) to reflect market diversity.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would purchase within 12 weeks") and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Hobby vs Sustainability Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a home spinning kit (specifying Rieter technology) and are randomly assigned to either a hobby-focused version (emphasizing creative fun and ease of use) or a sustainability-focused version (emphasizing recycled yarn and eco-credentials). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this kit at a price of €400?" (yes/no).
X1.sample: 300 crafters and hobbyists recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced for age and gender.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as a hobby (e.g., >40% say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as eco-friendly (e.g., >40% say yes).

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants who would purchase the kit under hobby messaging exceeds the proportion under sustainability messaging by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite is true, proceed to develop a sustainability-focused

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who seek creative outlets and unique fiber experiences.
final.value_proposition: A branded home spinning kit that combines Rieter technology with a hobby-focused experience, sold directly to consumers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and budget of €15,000, measuring purchase intent under hobby and sustainability messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (consumer demand for hobby spinning) and T2 (consumer demand for recycled fiber) remain uncertain due to limited public evidence. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the hobby‑focused kit exceeds the sustainability‑focused kit by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a hobby‑focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or the sustainability‑focused kit outperforms, reconsider the consumer proposition or explore other B2B value‑add services.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Hobby vs Sustainability Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a home spinning kit (specifying Rieter technology) and are randomly assigned to either a hobby-focused version (emphasizing creative fun and ease of use) or a sustainability-focused version (emphasizing recycled yarn and eco-credentials). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this kit at a price of €400?" (yes/no).
X1.sample: 300 crafters and hobbyists recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced for age and gender.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as a hobby (e.g., >40% say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as eco-friendly (e.g., >40% say yes).

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants who would purchase the kit under hobby messaging exceeds the proportion under sustainability messaging by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite is true, proceed to develop a sustainability-focused

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the theories under review. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who seek creative outlets and unique fiber experiences.
final.value_proposition: A branded home spinning kit that simplifies the creative process, offering a fun, affordable entry point into spinning with Rieter technology.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 300 crafters and hobbyists, to compare purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a home spinning kit. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the hobby-focused kit exceeds the sustainability-focused kit by at least 10 percentage points, we would proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or the sustainability-focused kit outperforms, we would reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must come from public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B product portfolio and market presence.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., professional contractors purchasing for residential projects).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.
4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.
assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.
Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.
Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.

T2.claim: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships.
T2.who_benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.
assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.
Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.
Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.
Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must come from public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B product portfolio and market presence.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., professional contractors purchasing for residential projects).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.
4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.
assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.
Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.
Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.

T2.claim: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships.
T2.who_benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.
assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.
Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.
Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.
Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience.
T2.first_claim: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test: Sika vs Generic Store Brand
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika-branded DIY sealant (highlighting ease-of-use, professional-grade results, and code compliance for residential use). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this product for a home improvement project?" (Yes/No). A control group views the same product description but without any branding (generic store brand).
X1.sample: 300 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage saying "Yes") for Sika-branded product versus generic store brand.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Sika-branded product will achieve a purchase intent rate at least 15 percentage points higher than the generic store brand.
prediction_by_theory.T2: No significant difference in purchase intent between Sika-branded and generic store brand (difference <5 percentage points).

X1.name: Digital Refund vs Public Placement Choice Experiment
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to digital refund/map proposition (T1) or public placement/digital refund proposition (T2). Participants view a mock consumer reverse vending machine and are asked to indicate whether they would use it and, if yes, whether they would prefer a digital refund or a physical refund. They also rate perceived convenience and likelihood to visit a public location.
X1.sample: 500 Norwegian consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who select "Would use" for each proposition. Secondary outcomes: (a) preference for digital vs physical refund (binary); (b) perceived convenience (1‑10 scale); (c) likelihood to visit a public location (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Proportion who select "Would use" for public placement proposition will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for digital refund proposition.

arguments.name: Digital Refund vs Public Placement Choice Experiment
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to digital refund/map proposition (T1) or public placement/digital refund proposition (T2). Participants view a mock consumer reverse vending machine and are asked to indicate whether they would use it and, if yes, whether they would prefer a digital refund or a physical refund. They also rate perceived convenience and likelihood to visit a public location.
arguments.sample: 500 Norwegian consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who select "Would use" for each proposition. Secondary outcomes: (a) preference for digital vs physical refund (binary); (b) perceived convenience (1‑10 scale); (c) likelihood to visit a public location (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Proportion who select "Would use" for public placement proposition will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for digital refund proposition.

arguments.method: Run two identical pilot sites in the same geographic area (e.g., a shopping mall) for 12 weeks. Both sites offer a TOMRA consumer RVM with a mobile app for drop‑off and digital refund. In Site A, the refund is paid directly via the app (no retailer partner). In Site B, the refund is linked to a retailer‑specific loyalty program that offers points redeemable for discounts at that retailer. Track the number of containers returned per week and the redemption rate of points (if any).
arguments.sample: Each site serves approximately 5,000 unique shoppers per week (total 10,000 per 12 weeks).
arguments.measure: Return rate per week (containers dropped off) and redemption rate of retailer points (if applicable).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Site A return rate will be at least 15% higher than baseline RVM return rates in comparable locations (e.g., 15% vs 10%).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Site B redemption rate will be at least 15% higher than baseline RVM redemption rates for existing retailer‑linked programs (e.g., 15% vs 10%).

arguments.decision_rule: If Site A return rate ≥ 15% and Site B redemption rate ≤ 10%, conclude T1 is better supported. If neither meets thresholds, the evidence is insufficient to justify expansion.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE concerns installation friction and does not address consumer purchase drivers (brand trust, performance, compatibility). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
final.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
final.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand for a premium proposition or for a specialized compatible solution. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
arguments.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

arguments.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE concerns installation friction and does not address consumer purchase drivers (brand trust, performance, compatibility). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, reliable solution for a specific use case (e.g., home EV charging comfort), because they trust the brand’s automotive heritage and are willing to pay a premium for performance and safety.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
arguments.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
arguments.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
arguments.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand for a premium proposition or for a specialized compatible solution. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
