X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE concerns installation friction and does not address consumer purchase drivers (brand trust, performance, compatibility). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
final.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
final.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand for a premium proposition or for a specialized compatible solution. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE concerns installation friction and does not address consumer purchase drivers (brand trust, performance, compatibility). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, reliable solution for a specific use case (e.g., home EV charging comfort), because they trust the brand’s automotive heritage and are willing to pay a premium for performance and safety.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
arguments.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
arguments.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
arguments.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand for a premium proposition or for a specialized compatible solution. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether Eberspächer Gruppe GmbH & Co. KG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B exhaust technology, vehicle heaters, and thermal management systems, and identify evidence that would justify such an investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider the company’s existing B2B focus, revenue base (€5.0 billion in 2025), and current reach to individual buyers (unknown).
Alternatives must include no expansion, product redesign, new route to buyers, and targeting a different customer group.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., electric vehicle (EV) thermal management for home charging, outdoor recreation, or fleet operators).
2) Expand B2B offerings by adding new product features or services without targeting individual consumers.
3) No expansion – maintain current product and market focus.
4) Target individual buyers directly with a consumer product line (e.g., aftermarket EV heaters, portable thermal solutions).
5) Partner with retailers or direct‑to‑consumer channels to reach individual buyers without direct manufacturing.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, reliable solution for a specific use case (e.g., home EV charging comfort), because they trust the brand’s automotive heritage and are willing to pay a premium for performance and safety.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking comfortable, reliable thermal management for electric vehicles at home.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view Eberspächer as a trusted automotive supplier that offers superior performance and reliability, they will choose its products over generic alternatives, even at a higher price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Eberspächer captures value by selling premium-priced consumer products directly or through specialty retailers, leveraging its existing B2B brand reputation to command higher margins.
assumptions: Consumers associate Eberspächer with automotive quality and reliability.
There is a market segment willing to pay a premium for EV home comfort solutions.
Eberspächer can manufacture or source consumer-grade products at a cost that allows a premium price.
predictions: In a test offering a premium consumer product (e.g., a high‑efficiency home EV heater) at a price 20% above competitors, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than for a generic alternative.
Surveyed consumers will cite brand trust and performance as primary reasons for choosing Eberspächer over alternatives.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s differentiated consumer proposition if they need a specific use case (e.g., home EV charging comfort) and discover that Eberspächer offers the only solution that meets their exact requirements, because they value compatibility with existing systems and reliability.
T2.who_benefits: Individual consumers who own electric vehicles and require reliable thermal management for home charging.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers identify Eberspächer as the only supplier with a product that seamlessly integrates with their EV charging setup and provides proven performance, they will choose it over competitors offering less compatible alternatives.

X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

X1.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE concerns installation friction and does not address consumer purchase drivers (brand trust, performance, compatibility). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
final.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
final.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand for a premium proposition or for a specialized compatible solution. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
arguments.sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.

arguments.decision_rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE concerns installation friction and does not address consumer purchase drivers (brand trust, performance, compatibility). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, reliable solution for a specific use case (e.g., home EV charging comfort), because they trust the brand’s automotive heritage and are willing to pay a premium for performance and safety.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus.
arguments.target_customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).
arguments.value_proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.
arguments.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand for a premium proposition or for a specialized compatible solution. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).
If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).
If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring can price its tools competitively while maintaining its premium reputation, generating revenue from a new consumer segment without diluting its brand in the industrial market.

X1.name: Hobbyist Price Sensitivity Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from hobbyist CNC forums (e.g., Tormach, CNCZone) and offered a Gühring drill bit at a price 10‑20% below its usual retail price (e.g., €150 instead of €180). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase it and, if so, the maximum price they would pay. The test runs for 4 weeks, with 200 participants expected to complete the survey.
X1.sample: 200 hobbyists who have posted about CNC projects in the past 12 months, recruited via forum announcements and social media.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: self‑reported importance of compatibility with existing CNC machines (1‑5 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and compatibility will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 60% of those who would buy.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and brand prestige will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 40% of those who would buy.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent ≥ 30% AND compatibility ranks ≥ 60% of purchase‑intent group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing compatibility. final.recommendation: Run the proposed Hobbyist Price Sensitivity Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity among hobbyists. If the test meets the decision rule (purchase intent ≥30% and compatibility ranks ≥60% of purchase-intent group), develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing compatibility. If not, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor hobbyist market trends.
final.target_customer: Hobbyist CNC users (home workshops, small businesses) who need precision metalworking tools and value compatibility with existing CNC machines.
final.value_proposition: A line of Gühring precision tools marketed as affordable, reliable, and compatible with popular CNC machines, enabling hobbyists to achieve professional-grade results without high-end prices.
final.next_action: Execute the 4‑week online survey with 200 hobbyists, offering a discounted drill bit and measuring purchase intent and compatibility ranking.
final.uncertainty: The test is the only way to confirm whether hobbyists will adopt Gühring at a price 10‑20% below premium brands and whether compatibility is the primary purchase driver.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent <30% or prestige ranks ≥40% of purchase-intent group, shift to a premium branding strategy.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-GUEHRING-UPDATE concerns a durability guarantee for a diamond-tipped nozzle, not Gühring’s precision tools. It does not address hobbyist purchase drivers, price sensitivity, or compatibility, which are central to T1. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.
arguments.new_claim: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they perceive them as affordable, reliable, and compatible with existing CNC machines, because these attributes lower the perceived risk and cost of switching from other brands.

arguments.recommendation: Run the proposed Hobbyist Price Sensitivity Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity among hobbyists. If the test meets the decision rule (purchase intent ≥30% and compatibility ranks ≥60% of purchase-intent group), develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing compatibility. If not, maintain the current B2B focus and monitor hobbyist market trends.
arguments.target_customer: Hobbyist CNC users (home workshops, small businesses) who need precision metalworking tools and value compatibility with existing CNC machines.
arguments.value_proposition: A line of Gühring precision tools marketed as affordable, reliable, and compatible with popular CNC machines, enabling hobbyists to achieve professional-grade results without high-end prices.
arguments.next_action: Execute the 4‑week online survey with 200 hobbyists, offering a discounted drill bit and measuring purchase intent and compatibility ranking.
arguments.uncertainty: The test is the only way to confirm whether hobbyists will adopt Gühring at a price 10‑20% below premium brands and whether compatibility is the primary purchase driver.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent <30% or prestige ranks ≥40% of purchase-intent group, shift to a premium branding strategy.
If additional evidence shows hobbyists already purchase Gühring at high volumes or that brand prestige drives sales, the recommendation would shift toward expanding the existing B2B model.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring can price its tools competitively while maintaining its premium reputation, generating revenue from a new consumer segment without diluting its industrial brand.

predictions: If offered at a price 10‑20% below premium CNC tool brands, Gühring will achieve at least 5% market share among hobbyists within 12 months.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. arguments.name: Premium vs Professional-Grade Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Gühring drill bit marketed as either (A) premium, high‑performance metalworking tool for hobbyists/small workshops (T1) or (B) professional‑grade tool for demanding projects (T2). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale and purchase intent (1‑10).
arguments.sample: 200 participants: 100 self‑identified hobbyists/small workshop owners (recruited via metalworking forums and social media) and 100 professionals (recruited via industry associations and LinkedIn). Randomly assign each participant to one of two message versions.
arguments.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and average purchase intent score for each message version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists exposed to premium messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to professional messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professionals exposed to professional messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to premium messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for premium messaging exceeds professional messaging by at least 15% (or purchase intent by at least 10 points on the 1‑10 scale) among hobbyists, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If the opposite holds for professionals, proceed to develop a professional‑grade consumer proposition. If neither

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on the existing B2B product portfolio and explore a low‑cost test (e.g., a limited launch of a premium‑priced kit) to gather real demand data before committing resources.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1, and the theory remains unchanged.

tool_result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

There is measurable demand for precision metalworking tools among this segment.
predictions: If offered at a 20 % premium over generic alternatives, at least 10 % of surveyed hobbyists will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a Krones home brewing kit described as either premium (professional-grade, signal expertise) or scalable (upgradeable, grow production). They are asked about willingness to pay and purchase intent. The test also collects demographic data (age, brewing experience) and willingness to invest in upgrades.
X1.sample: 200 home brewers recruited via hobbyist forums and social media, balanced across experience levels (novice, intermediate, expert).
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1‑“Very unlikely” to 7‑“Very likely”). Secondary measure: maximum price participants would pay.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated test (SYN-KRONES-UPDATE) measures the impact of cleaning burden on purchase choice among hobby/craft brewers, which is relevant to T1's premise that premium positioning signals expertise and quality. The test does not address T1's claim about price sensitivity or direct-to-consumer sales channels, but it does not contradict T1 either. Therefore, T1 remains supported by the evidence available.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

They are shown two Krones equipment options: a generic home-brew machine priced at $1,500 and a Krones professional-grade machine priced at $2,500 (or $2,200 with a premium finish). result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated test (SYN-KRONES-UPDATE) measures the impact of cleaning burden on purchase choice, which is relevant to T1's premise that homebrewers seek professional-grade performance reducing waste. The test shows automated cleaning increases choice, supporting the idea that performance advantages drive willingness to pay a premium.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to validate demand for a premium smart home kit versus a DIY kit before committing resources. The test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for Lapp’s cables and connectors for home automation and whether safety certification and DIY compatibility drive purchase decisions.

frame.objective: Determine whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial B2B focus, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home automation, automotive aftermarket, or consumer electronics).
2) Expand the existing industrial proposition into adjacent B2B segments (e.g., healthcare, renewable energy, or advanced robotics) without creating a distinct consumer offering.
3) Maintain the current business model and not pursue any expansion, focusing exclusively on industrial customers.
4) License or partner with consumer brands to embed Lapp components in consumer products, leveraging existing manufacturing capacity.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp's cables and connectors for home automation if they perceive them as premium, reliable, and integrated into smart home ecosystems, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners seeking reliable, integrated smart home components.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view Lapp components as essential for a secure, future-proof smart home, they will prioritize quality and brand reputation over price, shifting from generic to premium suppliers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp can charge premium prices for high-margin, integrated smart home kits and capture recurring revenue through accessories and service contracts.
assumptions: Consumers in target markets (e.g., Europe, North America) have sufficient disposable income to afford premium smart home components.
Lapp can develop or partner to integrate its cables into popular smart home platforms (e.g., Apple HomeKit, Google Nest).
Brand awareness of Lapp among consumers is sufficient to differentiate it from competitors.
predictions: In a test offering a Lapp-branded smart home kit at a 20% premium price compared to generic alternatives, at least 30% of target consumers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Repeat purchase intent for accessories will be at least 15% higher than for generic alternatives.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp's cables and connectors for home automation if they perceive them as premium, reliable, and integrated into smart home ecosystems, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Lapp's cables and connectors for home automation primarily because they need reliable, certified components for DIY projects and home improvement, not because of premium branding.
T2.who_benefits: DIY homeowners and home improvement enthusiasts who value safety, compliance, and compatibility.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view Lapp components as meeting or exceeding safety standards (e.g., UL, CE) and as compatible with popular DIY platforms (e.g., Arduino, Raspberry Pi), they will choose Lapp over generic brands even if price is comparable.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Lapp can sell through retail channels and online marketplaces at competitive prices, capturing volume sales and potentially licensing its connector designs to DIY brands.
assumptions: DIY consumers in target markets have access to information about safety certifications and compatibility.
Lapp can scale production to meet retail demand without compromising quality.
Retail partners will stock Lapp products if they meet DIY consumer needs.
predictions: In a test offering a Lapp-branded DIY kit at a price comparable to generic alternatives, at least 25% of target consumers will purchase within 12 weeks.
Repeat purchase intent for accessories will be at least 10% higher than for generic alternatives.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium Smart Home vs. DIY Kit
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 self-identified DIY enthusiasts (age 25-55, UK/DE/FR) and 250 smart home early adopters (age 25-45, same regions). Recruited via panel providers.
X1.measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for a premium-branded smart home kit (Lapp) vs. a comparable generic kit. 2) Purchase intent for a DIY kit (Lapp) vs. a comparable generic kit. 3) Willingness to pay for safety certification (UL/CE) and compatibility with popular DIY platforms (Arduino, Raspberry Pi).

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-LAPP-UPDATE concerns compatibility uncertainty for electric-car owners purchasing home charging cables, not consumer demand for premium smart home kits. It does not address T1's claim about premium branding or T2's claim about DIY compatibility. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial B2B focus, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.

Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home automation, automotive aftermarket, or consumer electronics).
2) Expand the existing industrial proposition into adjacent B2B segments (e.g., healthcare, renewable energy, or advanced robotics) without creating a distinct consumer offering.
3) Maintain the current business model and not pursue any expansion, focusing exclusively on industrial customers.
4) License or partner with consumer brands to embed Lapp components in consumer products, leveraging existing manufacturing capacity.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from generic cables to integrated, brand‑trusted components when the total cost of ownership (TCO) is perceived as lower due to reliability, warranty, and ecosystem compatibility.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp captures value through higher margin sales of integrated kits, subscription services for software updates, and data‑driven services that leverage consumer data.

Distribution channels (e.g., online retailers, specialty stores) will stock Lapp kits if they meet quality and integration standards.
predictions: In a test offering a Lapp‑branded smart home kit (e.g., power strip with integrated connectors) at a 20% price premium compared to generic alternatives, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15 percentage points higher.
Repeat purchase rate for Lapp kits will be at least 20% within 12 months, indicating consumer willingness to buy multiple integrated products.

Lapp can obtain necessary safety certifications for consumer products without major redesign.
Retailers will stock Lapp safety kits if they meet compliance standards.

Repeat purchase rate for Lapp safety kits will be at least 15% within 12 months, indicating consumer willingness to buy multiple safety‑certified products.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Safety-Certified Smart Home Kits
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.
X1.sample: 500 German consumers aged 25-55 who have purchased home automation products in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (percentage willing to buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) for two kit options: (1) Lapp premium smart home kit (integrated connectors, brand trust, design) priced at 20% premium over generic alternatives; (2) Lapp safety-certified kit (UL/CE compliance, safety messaging) priced at 15% premium over generic alternatives.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the premium kit will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for the safety-certified kit, and WTP for the premium kit will be at least 10% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the safety-certified kit will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for the premium kit, and WTP for the safety-certified kit will be at least 10% higher.

X1.decision_rule: If premium kit purchase intent ≥ 15 percentage points higher than safety kit → proceed with premium consumer proposition. If safety kit purchase intent ≥ 15 percentage points higher than premium kit → proceed with safety-certified consumer proposition. If neither condition met →

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-LAPP-UPDATE concerns compatibility uncertainty affecting purchase decisions for a specific product (home charging cable). It does not address consumer demand for premium, reliable components or safety certification, which are central to T1. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for premium vs safety-certified kits before committing resources.
final.target_customer: German consumers aged 25-55 who have purchased home automation products in the past 12 months.
final.value_proposition: Premium, integrated smart home kits leveraging Lapp’s industrial reliability and brand trust, sold through existing sales channels at a 20% price premium over generic alternatives.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 budget to recruit 500 participants and collect purchase intent and willingness to pay data for premium and safety-certified kits.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (consumer demand for premium, reliable components) and T2 (consumer demand for safety-certified components) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence from public sources.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the premium kit is at least 15 percentage points higher than for the safety kit, proceed with the premium consumer proposition.
If the test shows purchase intent for the safety kit is at least 15 percentage points higher than for the premium kit, proceed with the safety-certified consumer proposition.
If neither condition is met, reconsider any consumer expansion.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Professional-Grade vs Health-Focused Vacuum Sealer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two product descriptions: (A) Professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing; (B) Health-focused vacuum sealer marketed for nutrient retention and waste reduction. Both descriptions include price point (€200). Participants indicate whether they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. The
X1.sample: 500 German adults aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each product description, and binary purchase intent (yes/no).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average WTP for professional-grade description will be at least €200 and significantly higher than for health-focused description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP for health-focused description will be at least €200 and significantly higher than for professional-grade description.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE concerns running costs and does not address willingness to pay for a professional-grade vacuum sealer. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey (X1) to test whether consumers will pay a premium for a professional-grade vacuum sealer versus a health-focused one. The test will decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks, or to remain focused on B2B packaging equipment.
final.target_customer: German home cooks and culinary enthusiasts aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year.
final.value_proposition: A professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed as a reliable, airtight tool for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, positioned as a premium, high-performance kitchen appliance.
final.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €15,000 survey with 500 participants, presenting two product descriptions and measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay for professional-grade or health-focused vacuum sealers. The survey will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay for the professional-grade description exceeds €200 and is significantly higher than for the health-focused description, T1 would be supported and the consumer proposition would proceed.
If the opposite pattern emerges, T2 would be supported and a health‑focused proposition would be considered.
If neither difference meets the €20 threshold, both theories would remain unsupported and the recommendation would be to maintain B2B focus.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE concerns running costs and does not address willingness to pay for a professional-grade vacuum sealer. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a professional-grade tool that improves food freshness and reduces waste, leading to multiple purchases per household.

arguments.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey (X1) to test whether consumers will pay a premium for a professional-grade vacuum sealer versus a health-focused one. The test will decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks, or to remain focused on B2B packaging equipment.
arguments.target_customer: German home cooks and culinary enthusiasts aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year.
arguments.value_proposition: A professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed as a reliable, airtight tool for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, positioned as a premium, high-performance kitchen appliance.
arguments.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €15,000 survey with 500 participants, presenting two product descriptions and measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay for professional-grade or health-focused vacuum sealers. The survey will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay for the professional-grade description exceeds €200 and is significantly higher than for the health-focused description, T1 would be supported and the consumer proposition would proceed.
If the opposite pattern emerges, T2 would be supported and a health‑focused proposition would be considered.
If neither difference meets the €20 threshold, both theories would remain unsupported and the recommendation would be to maintain B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, small‑batch medical supplies) with a new product or service.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical, pharmaceutical, and industrial producers.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE concerns running costs and does not address willingness to pay for a professional-grade vacuum sealer. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

arguments.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey (X1) to test whether consumers will pay a premium for a professional-grade vacuum sealer versus a health-focused one. The test will decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks, or to remain focused on B2B packaging equipment.
arguments.target_customer: German home cooks and culinary enthusiasts aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year.
arguments.value_proposition: A professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed as a reliable, airtight tool for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, positioned as a premium, high-performance kitchen appliance.
arguments.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €15,000 survey with 500 participants, presenting two product descriptions and measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay for professional-grade or health-focused vacuum sealers. The survey will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay for the professional-grade description exceeds €200 and is significantly higher than for the health-focused description, T1 would be supported and the consumer proposition would proceed.
If the opposite pattern emerges, T2 would be supported and a health‑focused proposition would be considered.
If neither difference meets the €20 threshold, both theories would remain unsupported and the recommendation would be to maintain B2B focus.
