tool_result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

The test will decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks, or to remain focused on B2B packaging equipment.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, small‑batch medical supplies) with a new product or service.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical, pharmaceutical, and industrial producers.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in sous vide cooking and bulk food processing creates a demand for reliable, airtight sealing; current chamber sealers are already used by professional chefs and home enthusiasts, signaling quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC can price the consumer model at a premium (e.g., €200-€300) and sell accessories (bags, seals) and service contracts, generating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Home users have sufficient disposable income to justify the price.
Marketing can effectively communicate professional-grade performance.
Distribution channels (online, specialty retailers) can reach target consumers.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer.
Purchase intent will be higher when described as a professional-grade tool.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months.

X1.sample: 500 German adults aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for each product description, and binary purchase intent (yes/no).

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE concerns running costs and does not address willingness to pay for a professional-grade vacuum sealer. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey (X1) to test whether consumers will pay a premium for a professional-grade vacuum sealer versus a health-focused one. The test will decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks, or to remain focused on B2B packaging equipment.
final.target_customer: German home cooks and culinary enthusiasts aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year.
final.value_proposition: A professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed as a reliable, airtight tool for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, positioned as a premium, high-performance kitchen appliance.
final.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €15,000 survey with 500 participants, presenting two product descriptions and measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay for professional-grade or health-focused vacuum sealers. The survey will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay for the professional-grade description exceeds €200 and is significantly higher than for the health-focused description, T1 would be supported and the consumer proposition would proceed.
If the opposite pattern emerges, T2 would be supported and a health‑focused proposition would be considered.
If neither difference meets the €20 threshold, both theories would remain unsupported and the recommendation would be to maintain B2B focus.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE concerns running costs and does not address willingness to pay for a professional-grade vacuum sealer. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a professional-grade tool that improves food freshness and reduces waste, leading to multiple purchases per household.

arguments.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey (X1) to test whether consumers will pay a premium for a professional-grade vacuum sealer versus a health-focused one. The test will decide whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home cooks, or to remain focused on B2B packaging equipment.
arguments.target_customer: German home cooks and culinary enthusiasts aged 25-55 who have purchased home kitchen appliances in the past year.
arguments.value_proposition: A professional-grade vacuum sealer marketed as a reliable, airtight tool for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, positioned as a premium, high-performance kitchen appliance.
arguments.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €15,000 survey with 500 participants, presenting two product descriptions and measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay for professional-grade or health-focused vacuum sealers. The survey will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay for the professional-grade description exceeds €200 and is significantly higher than for the health-focused description, T1 would be supported and the consumer proposition would proceed.
If the opposite pattern emerges, T2 would be supported and a health‑focused proposition would be considered.
If neither difference meets the €20 threshold, both theories would remain unsupported and the recommendation would be to maintain B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial spinning equipment, components, and after-sales services.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.

Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and Rieter’s ability to reach consumers.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual buyers (e.g., home textile spinning kits, DIY fiber preparation systems).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding value-added services or new product modules for existing mill customers.

4) License Rieter’s spinning technology to third-party consumer brands rather than selling under Rieter’s own consumer brand.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home spinning kits if they view spinning as a creative hobby, and Rieter can capture value by selling branded kits and premium accessories through its own consumer channel.
T1.who_benefits: Individual crafters and hobbyists who seek creative outlets and unique fiber experiences.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growth in craft yarn purchases (e.g., crocheting) and interest in DIY fiber preparation indicate a segment willing to invest in spinning as a hobby. If Rieter offers a differentiated kit that simplifies the process and aligns with craft
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells branded spinning kits, accessories, and optional services (e.g., online tutorials, support) directly to consumers, earning higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Consumers perceive spinning as a fun, creative activity rather than a purely industrial process.
Rieter can design a kit that is easy to use and aesthetically appealing for home settings.
There is sufficient demand to justify a dedicated consumer channel.
predictions: If a test kit is offered at a price point of €300-€500, at least 10% of interested crafters will purchase within 12 weeks.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Hobby vs Sustainability Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a home spinning kit (specifying Rieter technology) and are randomly assigned to either a hobby-focused version (emphasizing creative fun and ease of use) or a sustainability-focused version (emphasizing recycled yarn and eco-credentials). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this kit at a price of €400?" (yes/no).
X1.sample: 300 crafters and hobbyists recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced for age and gender.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as a hobby (e.g., >40% say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as eco-friendly (e.g., >40% say yes).

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants who would purchase the kit under hobby messaging exceeds the proportion under sustainability messaging by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite is true, proceed to develop a sustainability-focused

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-RIETER-UPDATE concerns a hobby spinning machine offer with instructor training versus a manual-only version, and it shows a higher deposit rate for the training offer. This does not address consumer demand for recycled fiber or sustainability messaging, which are central to T2. Therefore T1 is unaffected by the simulated evidence and remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who seek creative outlets and unique fiber experiences.
final.value_proposition: A branded home spinning kit that combines Rieter technology with a user-friendly interface, sold directly to consumers at a premium price, leveraging the company’s existing GRS-certified recycling focus to differentiate.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, allocate €15,000 to recruit 300 crafters, create mock‑ups, and collect purchase intent data.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence that consumers will adopt home spinning kits, nor that they will prefer a hobby‑focused message over sustainability messaging.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the hobby‑focused kit exceeds the sustainability‑focused kit by at least 10 percentage points, we would proceed to develop a hobby‑focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or the sustainability‑focused kit outperforms, we would reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Hobby vs Sustainability Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a home spinning kit (specifying Rieter technology) and are randomly assigned to either a hobby-focused version (emphasizing creative fun and ease of use) or a sustainability-focused version (emphasizing recycled yarn and eco-credentials). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this kit at a price of €400?" (yes/no).
arguments.sample: 300 crafters and hobbyists recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced for age and gender.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as a hobby (e.g., >40% say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as eco-friendly (e.g., >40% say yes).

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants who would purchase the kit under hobby messaging exceeds the proportion under sustainability messaging by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite is true, proceed to develop a sustainability-focused

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-RIETER-UPDATE concerns a hobby spinning machine offer with instructor training versus a manual-only version, and it shows a higher deposit rate for the training offer. This does not address consumer demand for recycled fiber or sustainability messaging, which are central to T2. Therefore T1 is unaffected by the simulated evidence and remains unchanged.
arguments.new_claim: Consumers will adopt home spinning kits if they view spinning as a creative hobby, and Rieter can capture value by selling branded kits and premium accessories through its own consumer channel.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.
arguments.target_customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who seek creative outlets and unique fiber experiences.
arguments.value_proposition: A branded home spinning kit that combines Rieter technology with a user-friendly interface, sold directly to consumers at a premium price, leveraging the company’s existing GRS-certified recycling focus to differentiate.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, allocate €15,000 to recruit 300 crafters, create mock‑ups, and collect purchase intent data.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence that consumers will adopt home spinning kits, nor that they will prefer a hobby‑focused message over sustainability messaging.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the hobby‑focused kit exceeds the sustainability‑focused kit by at least 10 percentage points, we would proceed to develop a hobby‑focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or the sustainability‑focused kit outperforms, we would reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who seek creative outlets and unique fiber experiences.
final.value_proposition: A branded home spinning kit that combines Rieter technology with a simple, fun user experience, sold directly to consumers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 crafters, randomizing between hobby and sustainability messaging, to determine which messaging drives higher purchase intent.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Hobby vs Sustainability Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a home spinning kit (specifying Rieter technology) and are randomly assigned to either a hobby-focused version (emphasizing creative fun and ease of use) or a sustainability-focused version (emphasizing recycled yarn and eco-credentials). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this kit at a price of €400?" (yes/no).
arguments.sample: 300 crafters and hobbyists recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced for age and gender.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as a hobby (e.g., >40% say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when kit is marketed as eco-friendly (e.g., >40% say yes).

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants who would purchase the kit under hobby messaging exceeds the proportion under sustainability messaging by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite is true, proceed to develop a sustainability-focused

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-RIETER-UPDATE concerns a hobby spinning machine offer with instructor training versus a manual-only version, and it shows that the instructor-training offer secured more paid deposits (32) than the manual-only offer (72). This does not address consumer demand for recycled fiber or sustainability messaging, but it does indicate that a skill barrier (instructor training) can influence purchase
arguments.new_claim: Consumers will adopt home spinning kits if they view spinning as a creative hobby and are willing to invest in learning, and Rieter can capture value by selling branded kits and premium accessories through its own consumer channel.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under hobby vs sustainability messaging before committing resources.
arguments.target_customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who seek creative outlets and unique fiber experiences.
arguments.value_proposition: A branded home spinning kit that combines Rieter technology with a simple, fun user experience, sold directly to consumers at a premium price.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 crafters, randomizing between hobby and sustainability messaging, to determine which messaging drives higher purchase intent.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 (consumer demand for hobby spinning) and T2 (consumer demand for recycled fiber) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the hobby-focused kit exceeds the sustainability-focused kit by at least 10 percentage points, we would proceed to develop a hobby-focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or the sustainability-focused kit outperforms, we would reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct the proposed 12‑week digital campaign test (X1) to measure homeowner conversion and willingness to pay. If the test meets the thresholds (conversion ≥ 10% and WTP ≥ €2,500), proceed to develop a consumer‑branded module for homeowners; otherwise, maintain current B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a specific consumer use case.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential partner/distribution relationships.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home storage, small‑business inventory management).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., food‑processing, e‑commerce fulfillment) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion – maintain current product and market focus, monitor consumer trends without investment.
4) License Kardex’s technology to consumer brands or white‑label solutions for consumer markets.

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Kardex’s automated storage solutions because they value space efficiency and convenience, leading to repeat purchases of additional modules for home storage.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking to maximize limited space and reduce manual storage effort.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of space constraints in modern housing and the convenience of automated retrieval reduce the perceived barrier to adopting new storage solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex can capture value through direct-to-consumer sales of consumer-branded modules, subscription services for automated retrieval, and premium pricing for space-saving design.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to allocate budget for automated storage beyond essential purchases.
Marketing can effectively communicate the value proposition to the homeowner segment.
Distribution channels exist to reach homeowners directly.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate intent to buy a Kardex module for home storage within 12 months.
Actual purchase conversion rate for homeowner-targeted campaigns will exceed 10% (based on a test of 100 homeowners).

T2.claim: Small businesses and startups will adopt Kardex’s automated storage solutions because they need flexible, scalable inventory management and Kardex’s modular systems provide a lower‑cost entry point compared to traditional warehousing.
T2.who_benefits: Small businesses and startups with limited capital and space, seeking efficient inventory storage and retrieval.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These businesses face high overhead costs and need to quickly adapt to market demand; Kardex’s modular approach allows them to scale up without large upfront investments.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Kardex can capture value through subscription‑based pricing for modules, service contracts for maintenance, and bundled packages with other business‑to‑business services.
assumptions: Small businesses are willing to invest in automated storage if it reduces operational costs.
Kardex can reach this segment through existing dealer network or new partnerships.
Regulatory compliance for small businesses is manageable with Kardex’s support.
predictions: Surveyed small businesses will indicate intent to purchase a Kardex module within 12 months.
Actual purchase conversion rate for small‑business targeted campaigns will exceed 8% (based on a test of 100 small businesses).

X1.name: Homeowner vs Small Business Digital Campaign Test
X1.method: Run two parallel digital campaigns targeting distinct segments: homeowners and small businesses. Each campaign will offer a limited‑time, discounted price for a Kardex consumer‑branded vertical lift module (VLM). Track conversion rate (purchase intent) and willingness to pay (WTP) within the 12‑week test period.
X1.sample: 1) Homeowner campaign: 1,000 Swiss homeowners (aged 25‑55) recruited via online panels, targeted based on self‑reported home storage needs and interest in smart home solutions. 2) Small Business campaign: 1,000 small business owners (50‑250 employees) recruited via business directories and industry forums, targeted based on self‑reported inventory management challenges and interest in automated storage.
X1.measure: 1) Conversion rate: percentage of exposed users who click "Learn More" and complete a purchase intent form. 2) Average willingness to pay (WTP): maximum price willing to pay for a 2‑unit module (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowner conversion rate ≥ 10% and average WTP ≥ EUR 2,500.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small Business conversion rate ≥ 8% and average WTP ≥ EUR 1,800.

X1.decision_rule: If homeowner conversion ≥ 10% AND average WTP ≥ EUR 2,500, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If small business conversion ≥ 8% AND average WTP ≥ EUR 1,800, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition targeting small businesses. If neither threshold met, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE concerns homeowner choice between rental and purchase of a compact automated storage module, indicating that upfront cost affects purchase decisions. This supports T1's premise that homeowners value space efficiency and will adopt automated storage if cost is removed as a barrier.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct the proposed 12‑week digital campaign test (X1) to measure homeowner conversion and willingness to pay. If the test meets the thresholds (conversion ≥ 10% and WTP ≥ €2,500), proceed to develop a consumer‑branded module for homeowners; otherwise, maintain current B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Homeowners seeking space‑efficient automated storage solutions.
final.value_proposition: A consumer‑branded, direct‑to‑consumer automated vertical lift module that eliminates upfront cost barriers, offering convenience, space savings, and a subscription‑based service model.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week digital campaign test (X1) with 1,000 Swiss homeowners, track conversion and willingness to pay, and decide on product development based on results.
final.uncertainty: Both homeowner demand and willingness to pay for a consumer‑branded module are uncertain; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows homeowner conversion ≥ 10% and average willingness to pay ≥ €2,500, the recommendation would shift to develop the consumer proposition.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt automated home storage if they perceive it as a premium, time‑saving solution, and are willing to pay a price premium for integrated, easy‑to‑use systems that reduce clutter and simplify inventory management.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking efficient home storage and willingness to pay for convenience; Kardex would capture value through higher‑margin consumer sales and subscription services.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from traditional storage solutions to automated systems when they experience the time and space savings, and when price sensitivity is offset by perceived long‑term convenience and reduced physical effort.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex would sell consumer‑branded modules or kits through retail or direct channels, charge monthly or annual fees for software/service, and potentially offer subscription bundles that include consumables.
assumptions: Consumers assess total cost of ownership (TCO) including installation, maintenance, and consumables.
Competition from low‑cost DIY storage solutions is limited.
Kardex can design a user‑friendly, aesthetically acceptable consumer product.
Distribution channels (retail, online) can be secured without major new investments.
predictions: A survey of 500 households would show >30% indicating intent to purchase an automated home storage system priced at 1.5x the cost of a comparable manual unit.
Purchase intent would correlate with self‑reported time savings and reduced clutter worries.
Actual purchase rate would be lower than intent due to price sensitivity, resulting in a conversion rate of ~15%.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt automated home storage if they perceive it as a premium, time‑saving solution, and are willing to pay a price premium for integrated, easy‑to‑use systems that reduce clutter and simplify inventory management.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt automated home storage if they receive it as a gift or subscription bundled with a home‑improvement service, leveraging existing relationships with retailers or subscription platforms to lower perceived risk and reduce upfront cost.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers gain convenient storage without upfront purchase; retailers gain incremental sales and subscription revenue; Kardex gains volume sales and recurring revenue through bundled offerings.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers adopt automated storage when it is presented as a low‑risk, bundled service that aligns with existing home‑improvement workflows, eliminating the need for large upfront cash outlay and reducing perceived complexity.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Kardex would partner with retailers or subscription platforms to offer consumer‑branded modules as part of a bundled kit, charging a subscription fee for software/service and consumables, and potentially selling hardware at a lower margin.
assumptions: Retailers or subscription platforms have existing customer databases and distribution channels.
Consumers trust bundled offerings from trusted home‑improvement brands.
Kardex can design a modular, easy‑to‑install system that fits standard home‑improvement packaging.
Subscription model provides predictable recurring revenue.
predictions: A survey of 500 households would show >25% indicating intent to purchase a bundled automated storage kit if offered through a home‑improvement retailer.
Purchase intent would be higher among households that have previously purchased home‑improvement products from the same retailer.
Actual purchase rate would be driven by subscription uptake, with a conversion rate of ~10% for bundled offers.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt automated home storage if they receive it as a gift or subscription bundled with a home‑improvement service, leveraging existing relationships with retailers or subscription platforms to lower perceived risk and reduce upfront cost.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Maintain current B2B focus and monitor consumer trends without investment. Run the proposed Home Storage Consumer Intent Test to gather real evidence before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a specific consumer use case.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential partner/distribution relationships.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home storage, small‑business inventory management).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., food‑processing, e‑commerce fulfillment) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion – maintain current product and market focus, monitor consumer trends without investment.
4) License Kardex’s technology to consumer brands or white‑label solutions for consumer markets.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems for home use if they perceive the solution as a premium, space‑saving product that reduces clutter and improves organization, and are willing to pay a price premium over traditional storage solutions.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners who need efficient storage for limited space and value convenience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view the system as a design‑focused, space‑saving solution that simplifies organization, they will switch from traditional storage to Kardex’s automated system, even at a higher price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex captures value by selling the system directly to consumers at premium prices, leveraging its brand reputation for quality and efficiency, and by offering subscription services for maintenance and upgrades.
assumptions: Consumers in target segments have sufficient disposable income to afford a premium automated storage solution.
The perceived benefits of reduced clutter and improved organization outweigh the higher cost.
Kardex can reach individual buyers through direct‑to‑consumer channels (e.g., e‑commerce, retail partnerships) without relying solely on B2B distribution.
predictions: In a test offering a home‑use version of Kardex’s vertical lift module at a 20% price premium, at least 15% of target consumers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Surveyed consumers will rank the system’s design and space‑saving benefits as top reasons for choosing Kardex over alternatives.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems for home use if they perceive the solution as a premium, space‑saving product that reduces clutter and improves organization, and are willing to pay a price premium over traditional storage solutions.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems for home use if they need a scalable, flexible solution for growing collections (e.g., books, toys, hobby supplies) and value the ability to easily retrieve and store items without manual sorting, even at a moderate price premium.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners with collections that require efficient storage and retrieval, particularly those with limited space and a need for adaptability.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers perceive the system as a scalable, low‑effort storage solution that keeps items organized without manual sorting, they will switch from traditional storage to Kardex’s automated system, even at a moderate price premium.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Kardex captures value by selling the system through consumer‑friendly e‑commerce channels at a premium price, emphasizing the ease of retrieval and scalability, and by offering optional add‑ons for specific collection types.
assumptions: Consumers in target segments have disposable income sufficient to afford a premium automated storage solution.
The need for scalable, low‑effort storage for growing collections is a primary purchase driver.
Kardex can reach individual buyers directly through online marketplaces and retail partnerships without relying solely on B2B channels.
predictions: In a test offering a home‑use version of Kardex’s vertical lift module at a 15% price premium, at least 10% of target consumers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Surveyed consumers will rank the system’s scalability and ease of retrieval as top reasons for choosing Kardex over alternatives.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems for home use if they need a scalable, flexible solution for growing collections (e.g., books, toys, hobby supplies) and value the ability to easily retrieve and store items without manual sorting, even at a moderate price premium.

X1.name: Home Storage Consumer Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 500 Swiss consumers aged 25-55, recruited via panel, balanced for gender and region.
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents who indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks at a 20% price premium (T1) and a 15% price premium (T2). Secondary measure: maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 15% of respondents will express intent to purchase at the 20% premium, and WTP will exceed €1,200.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 10% of respondents will express intent to purchase at the 15% premium, and WTP will exceed €900.

X1.decision_rule: If the observed intent rate for T1 ≥ 15% and T2 ≤ 10%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium home storage (T1). If T2 ≥ 10% and T1 ≤ 15%, develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting scalable, low‑effort storage for growing collections (T2). If neither condition is met, maintain current B2B focus and monitor consumer trends without investment.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE concerns a rental/purchase choice for a compact automated storage module and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the specific need for reduced clutter and improved organization. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and willingness-to-pay questions.
arguments.sample: 500 Swiss consumers aged 25-55, recruited via panel, balanced for gender and region.

If T2 ≥ 10% and T1 ≤ 15%, develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting scalable, low‑effort storage for growing collections (T2). If neither condition is met, maintain current B2B focus and monitor consumer trends without investment.

Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Sika’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must come from public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B product portfolio and market presence.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., professional contractors purchasing for residential projects).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.
4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.
assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.
Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.
Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.

T2.claim: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships.
T2.who_benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.
assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.
Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.
Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.
predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.
Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test: Sika vs Generic Store Brand
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika-branded DIY sealant (highlighting ease-of-use, professional-grade results, and code compliance for residential use). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this product for a home improvement project?" (Yes/No). A control group views the same product description but without any branding (generic store brand).
X1.sample: 300 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage saying "Yes") for Sika-branded product versus generic store brand.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for waste, metal recycling, mining, and food processing).
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.

alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential or small‑business deposit return, sold directly to consumers or via retailers.
2) Create a subscription‑based recycling service using TOMRA sensors to collect and sort consumer‑generated waste at home or in buildings.
3) Partner with retailers or housing associations to install TOMRA sensors in public spaces (e.g., shopping malls, office buildings) for consumer‑generated sorting and recycling.
4) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B customers and existing product lines.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Brembo investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B and aftermarket offerings, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Brembo’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of a new consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., high‑performance motorcycle brakes sold directly to enthusiasts).
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without differentiation (e.g., sell aftermarket brake kits through retail channels).
3) No expansion – maintain current B2B and aftermarket focus.
4) License Brembo’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under its own brand.

The market is large enough to justify dedicated consumer marketing and distribution.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are motorcycle enthusiasts (n=500) and urban/e-bike commuters (n=500). Each participant sees a product description of a high‑performance Brembo brake kit for their respective segment (e.g., GR‑PRO for mountain biking, XTRA Signature for e‑bike). The description includes price (e.g., €750 for GR‑PRO), performance claims, and a
X1.sample: 500 motorcycle enthusiasts (recruited via motorcycle forums and clubs) and 500 urban/e‑bike commuters (recruited via cycling groups and e‑bike forums). Stratify by region (Europe/North America) to reflect market diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as binary: "Would you buy this product within 12 months?" (yes/no). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of motorcycle enthusiasts will indicate purchase intent for the GR‑PRO kit, with a WTP average of €700‑€800.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 25% of urban/e‑bike commuters will indicate purchase intent for the XTRA Signature kit, with a WTP average of €350‑€450.
